pages.name: Valve shut
pages.task: This pump's head is 30 − 0.04q² metres, where q is its flow in L/s. With its discharge valve open, it settled at 22 m. Shut that valve fully while it runs. What head does it give now?
pages.why: No water can pass, so q is 0. And 30 − 0.04 × 0² is 30 m. The pump spins and pushes, but nothing flows. No path is open.

Note 1 says TV1 is drawn in its fail position. P1 is running and P2 stopped. TV1 is set to cooler. Every valve is open. No flow is shown yet.

pages.name: As drawn
pages.task: Every valve is drawn open. The labels under the pumps show the plant now. P1 is running and P2 is stopped. What is P2 doing?
pages.why: The sheet draws each valve in its normal position, unless a note says otherwise. Both of P2's valves are open. So it can start at once if P1 stops. That is a standby pump.

pages.name: Back through P2?
pages.task: P1 runs. P2 is stopped, with both its valves open. Does water run back through P2 to the suction?
pages.answer: No, its non-return valve stops it
pages.why: Water leaving P1 reaches the top of P2's branch at NR2. P1's discharge is at a higher pressure than the suction. So water would run back through P2 if it could. NR2 passes water only away from P2, so the branch stays still. Without it, some of P1's water would run back through P2 and miss the cooler.

pages.name: If the air fails
pages.task: TV1 is set some each way. Its diaphragm is worked by air. If the air supply fails, where does TV1 go?
pages.why: A diaphragm symbol does not say whether air opens or shuts a valve. So the symbol alone cannot tell you where TV1 goes when its air fails. Note 1 can. It says TV1 is drawn in its fail position, and it is drawn through the cooler. A three-way valve is sometimes drawn where it fails to, not where it normally sits. So read the notes before you trust its drawn position.

pages.name: Isolate P2
pages.task: P2's casing must be opened while P1 keeps running. Which valves would you shut?
pages.why: P2 has two pipes: its suction through V3, and its discharge through NR2 to V4. Shut and lock both valves, and lock off P2's starter. Then drain the casing and prove it at zero. P1 keeps the loop running throughout.

pages.name: Drawing against plant
pages.text: A drawing is only as good as its match with the plant. Before you trust it for an isolation, check every valve on the plant against it. The plant sketch sits beside the drawing. It is the same loop, with its pipes where they really run.

pages.name: One too many
pages.task: The plant has one valve the drawing does not show. Which one is it?
pages.answer: The valve with no tag, on the header tank's line
pages.why: It sits on the header tank's line, and it is shut. It cuts the loop off from its header tank. The drawing gives no sign of it. As the water warms, it expands. With nowhere to go, the loop's pressure climbs.

pages.name: A second path
pages.text: This sheet moves fuel from two storage tanks to a day tank. X1 is a cross-connection, drawn shut. It joins tank 2's line to the pump's suction. Open it, and P3 can draw from tank 2 as well. X1 is open and P3 is running. Fuel is lit from both tanks through S2, P3, NR3 and F3 into the day tank.

pages.name: Clean the strainer
pages.task: X1 is open, and P3 is stopped and locked off. You must open S2 to clean it. What is the smallest number of valves you must shut?
pages.why: Two lines reach S2 from before it. Tank 1's comes through F1, and tank 2's through X1. After S2, the line runs through the stopped P3 and NR3 to F3, with the day tank beyond. Shut F1, X1 and F3.

pages.name: Gate or globe?
pages.task: F1 and F3 are drawn with the same valve symbol. On the plant, F1 is a gate valve and F3 a globe valve. Where would the drawing tell you that?
pages.answer: In each valve's tag or the sheet's notes and legend
pages.why: Gate and globe valves are often drawn with the same symbol, so the symbol cannot tell them apart. The valve's tag or the sheet's notes and legend may say which it is. If nothing on the sheet says, check the valve on the plant.
